*Not every question in this template applies to every study, and some cannot be answered before the data are collected. Leaving a question open is acceptable. If you do, state briefly why. Where a choice depends on the data, consider pre-registering the decision rule instead of the decision itself.*

# Part A: General Information {.unnumbered .unlisted}

## Summary of the study

*Provide a summary of the whole study/survey and provide details that are relevant to understand the background of the study and survey in general. This can be extensive if necessary but should be kept brief.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
The study aims to estimate the value of urban green with different methods. A representative quota sample is taken from a panel with German adults from the fourteenth biggest cities in Germany. The survey has been conducted twice in 2020 and 2022. While the survey contains three valuation methods (hedonic pricing, life satisfaction, choice experiment), this pre-registration is only for the choice experiment. The questionnaire includes several other questions on socio-demographics, housing characteristics...
:::

## What are your research questions and/or hypotheses?

*Briefly but precisely state all research questions and hypotheses of this study. Hypotheses should be testable with the methods described later.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
H1: Living closer to an urban green space increases utility\
H2: People prefer more natural urban green spaces to less natural ones\
H3: People are willing to pay a higher rent for closer urban green spaces to their home and for more naturalness of this urban green space\
H4: Preferences for distance to urban green space and naturalness differ between cities and socio-demographics of respondents\
H5: Providing additional information on the effect of naturalness of urban green on the urban heat island effect increases the willingness to pay for more natural urban green spaces.\
H6: Providing additional information on the effect of naturalness of urban green on the urban heat island effect does not increase the willingness to pay for closer distances to the park.\
H7: Providing additional information on the effect of naturalness of urban green on the urban heat island effect does not change the marginal utility of income.
:::

## What is the format of the survey instrument?

*Elaborate on the survey instrument. Sub-questions could be: Is it online or offline? Is the survey programmed by you or by an external company? Who is collecting the data? How long is the questionnaire?*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
The survey is carried out online with a web questionnaire designed in “LimeSurvey”. The data is collected by the survey company “IMUG” from a representative panel provided by Gapfish.
:::

## Motivate and describe your sampling approach

*Describe your sampling strategy in detail and provide reasons for it. If it was not a random sample, why not? Are you using quotas to achieve a representative sample? Who is your target population? Do you use screening questions?*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
The sample should be representative at the country level with respect to gender, and age. We ensure this by using quotas. The sample only consists of people who live in a rented apartment or house. People who live in their own apartment or house were screened out at the beginning of the survey.
:::

## How did you incentivize your sample?

*Describe how respondents are compensated for completing the questionnaire. If you use individual incentives (e.g. as in a real choice experiment), explain how it works.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
Respondents receive a payment for completing the questionnaire. The payment procedure is handled by the survey company. We were not informed about the amount the respondents received for completing the survey.
:::

## How did you determine the sample size?

*State your target sample size and explain how you arrived at it. Four approaches are listed here -- from simple to more rigorous. State whether between-subject effects are included in the sample size calculation and whether power calculations used the same priors as the experimental design.*

*— **Budget or practical constraint**: If your sample size is restricted by budget or other constraints, state that here.  It is still worth doing a brief plausibility check using one of the methods below, e.g. to determine power for different effect sizes.*

*— **Rule of thumb**: A common minimum is $N \geq 500L_{max}/(JS)$, where $L_{max}$ is the largest number of levels for any attribute, $J$ is the number of alternatives (excluding none), and $S$ is the number of choice tasks per respondent [@Orme2010, p.64]. @Assele2023 propose an improved rule of $N \geq 150K/S$, where $K$ is the total number of parameters, which better accounts for model complexity and reduces underestimation compared to Orme's rule, particularly for larger designs. Note that both rules do not account for the desired power or significance level, and tend to underestimate N for mixed logit and latent class models [@Assele2023].*

*— **AVC-based power calculation**: The S-efficiency approach of @RoseBliemer2013 derives the minimum N for which all parameters achieve statistical significance from the asymptotic variance-covariance matrix of the target model, and is implemented as a design criterion in software such as NGENE or spdesign in R [@spdesign]. @deBekkerGrob2015 extend this to a full power calculation by additionally specifying a desired power level $1-\beta$, and provide a step-by-step guide with R code. These approaches only work if the design is known and rely on prior assumptions.*

*— **Simulation-based**: The most flexible approach. Simulate datasets under your assumed data-generating process (utility specification, error variance, parameter priors), estimate the target model, and iterate over values of N until the desired recovery rate or statistical power is achieved. This approach is particularly well-suited for complex models as it allows testing of any model including models with interaction terms, latent variables etc. In R, the `simulateDCE` package [@simulateDCE] supports this workflow.*

*Also state whether subgroup analyses require a larger N, and whether power calculations used the same priors as the experimental design.*


::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
Our target sample size is N = 800. The sample size is primarily constrained by the project budget. As a plausibility check, we applied the Johnson & Orme rule of thumb: with $t = 10$ choice tasks, $a = 3$ alternatives, and $c = 5$ levels (the maximum across attributes), the minimum sample size for a main-effects MNL model is $500 \times 5 \,/\, (10 \times 3) \approx 83$. Our target N substantially exceeds this minimum. We did not conduct a formal AVC-based or simulation-based power analysis, as the design was not finalised prior to sample size determination. For subgroup analyses by treatment arm (three groups), each group will contain approximately 267 respondents, which exceeds the commonly recommended minimum of 200 per group.
:::


## Did you conduct any pre-studies to develop the choice experiment and questionnaire?

*Describe the procedure to develop your questionnaire. This could include focus groups, expert interviews, a research project etc.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
We draw from the two earlier studies. The results from the earlier studies are published in Land Economics. The earlier studies were extensively pre-tested as described in the paper “The value of naturalness of urban green spaces: Evidence from a discrete choice experiment”:
“[...] the survey was pretested from the 15th of April 2020 to the 21st of April 2020 with 520 participants, of which 264 respondents answered the pretest completely. We used this pretest sample to assess the suitability of our survey, the comprehensibility of the questions, and to design the choice sets.”

and

“The graphical scale was originally developed by several expert panel meetings of biologists and economists to reflect an increasing index of biodiversity and ecosystem services (such as water purification and carbon sequestration). It was validated and slightly revised in the three focus group discussions, where respondents were asked among the others (i) “What do you understand by the term ‘naturalness’? (ii) “What characteristics does a near-natural green space have for you?” (iii) rank the five illustrations by the degree of naturalness.”


Bronnmann, Julia, Liebelt, Veronika, Marder, Fabian, Meya, Jasper and Quaas, Martin F., 2023 “The Value of Naturalness of Urban Green Spaces: Evidence From a Discrete Choice Experiment”, Land Economics  	



We have also conducted a pre-test with N=200. Based on the results, we slightly modified the questionnaire.

:::



## Define how you deal with outliers and how you exclude respondents/choices.

*Criteria to determine and exclude outliers should be specified before survey conduction. Criteria could be related for example to survey time. *

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
We exclude speeders. A respondent counts as a speeder if the total completion time is below one third of the median completion time in the realised sample, or if the respondent spends less than five seconds on more than half of the ten choice sets. We also exclude respondents who provide a monthly rent outside the range of 50€ to 15000€. Observations from respondents who did not complete the survey are not included. We report how many respondents each rule removes and re-estimate the main model on the unrestricted sample as a robustness check.

:::


## How do you deal with missing data?

*In surveys, some data points may be missing, e.g. if respondents do not answer a specific question. One can exclude such respondents or use imputation methods. Explain your strategy. *

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
The questionnaire requires an answer before a respondent can continue, so item non-response is limited to the optional income question. Where income is missing we drop the respondent from models using income, but keep them in all other models, and we report the resulting sample size per model.

:::

## Will you share the data and code after publication?

*Data and code sharing are essential for replicable research and strongly encouraged. 
Describe where you plan to make data and code available (e.g., OSF, Zenodo, GitHub, 
Harvard Dataverse). If sharing is not possible, provide a reason. Common restrictions 
include contractual obligations with survey companies, privacy regulations (e.g., GDPR), 
or confidentiality agreements. Consider whether anonymized data could be shared instead.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
We will publish the anonymized dataset and all analysis code (data preparation, design 
generation, estimation) on Zenodo and GitHub upon acceptance. A GDPR-compliant 
anonymized version of the data will be shared; researchers requiring the full dataset 
can request access via a data use agreement.
:::


## Will you share the survey instrument?

*The questionnaire and choice cards are essential for assessing validity and enabling 
replication. Describe whether and where you will share them (e.g., as a supplementary 
file, on OSF). Note any restrictions if the instrument is proprietary or licensed.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
The full questionnaire including screenshots of the choice cards will be published as 
a supplementary file with the paper and on OSF.
:::


## How do you plan to handle deviations from this pre-registration?
*A pre-registration records your intended design and analysis before the data are
collected. Because some things cannot be foreseen at this stage, you may later find
that a deviation is warranted. For example an unforeseen event during data
collection, an error or gap discovered in the plan, or an assumption (about
respondent behaviour, a distribution, or model convergence) that does not hold once
the data are in [@lakens2024]. Deviations are not in themselves a problem; what matters is that any deviation is reported transparently and kept distinct from the analyses you planned in advance. You are not asked to predict specific deviations. Instead, please state where and how you would document any deviation should one arise (e.g. an amendment to the registration, a supplementary file, or the paper
itself), noting briefly what was planned, what was done instead and why, and whether
the change weakens or strengthens the resulting conclusions.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
We do not anticipate major deviations from this plan. If deviations do occur, 
we will document each one in a supplementary file accompanying the analysis 
code, specifying what was planned, what was done instead, the reason for the 
change, and whether we judge the deviation to weaken or strengthen the test of 
the affected hypothesis. For example, if the achieved sample size in one of 
the 14 cities falls substantially short of the planned quota because the panel 
provider cannot recruit enough eligible respondents, we will report the 
achieved sample size, discuss the resulting loss in statistical power, and 
still estimate the pre-registered model on the available data rather than 
changing the model to compensate. Similarly, if we find during estimation that 
the assumed normal distribution for the naturalness parameter is implausible 
(e.g. based on diagnostic plots or convergence issues), we will additionally 
report results under a triangular distribution and discuss whether our 
conclusions on H1-H4 are sensitive to this choice.
:::



## Anything else you want to mention regarding survey information:

*A free text if anything important has not been captured so far.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
No additional remarks.
:::



# Part B: Experimental Design

The design stage includes selection of attributes, a clear definition of the choice situation and a statistical design. The design stage is critical to the choice experiment's validity and should be tested extensively. This template does not include best practices, it only serves as a reminder of the design stages. We highly recommend to align the research on @johnston2017contemporary and @mariel2021environmental. @johnston2017contemporary focuses on best practices for stated preference studies broadly, while @mariel2021environmental provides more hands-on guidance specific to discrete choice experiment design and implementation.

## Describe the choice situation or good to be valued

*Provide a detailed explanation of the choice situation. What is the good to be valued. How is the scope and time frame defined. For environmental economics applications, describe the extent of the proposed change and the extent of the market.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
In the setting of the choice experiment, the respondents are told that they should imagine that the local city authorities are planning to restructure the individually most visited urban green space of the respondent. The restructuring affects the naturalness of the green space and the walking distance to the green space. In the choice situation, the respondents can choose between the status quo and two alternative restructuring programs, which come with additional monthly costs via the incidental rental...
:::

## Which attributes (and respective levels) are you using?

*For each attribute in your survey, provide a clear and concise description, 
and explain each level if needed. Attributes and levels should reflect the 
information needs of decision-makers, importance to respondents, feasibility/credibility 
of implementation, and statistical efficiency. Attributes should be clearly defined and, where 
possible, vary independently of each other [@johnston2017contemporary]. 
Common approaches to identify and refine attributes include literature 
review, expert consultation, and focus groups or pre-testing 
[@mariel2021environmental]. A justification for the choices can also be provided here.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
The attributes were selected based on a review of the literature on urban 
green space valuation and on consultations with urban planners and 
landscape ecologists involved in the broader research project. Naturalness 
was included because it is most directly linked to the ecosystem co-benefits 
(e.g. urban heat mitigation) motivating the study, while distance and rent 
reflect standard accessibility and cost trade-offs familiar from housing 
choice. All three attributes vary independently of one another, since none 
is mechanically determined by the levels of the others. Comprehensibility of 
the attributes and levels, in particular the graphical naturalness scale, 
was confirmed in three focus groups (see Section "Did you conduct any 
pre-studies...").

The attributes are the naturalness of the urban green space, the walking 
distance to the urban green space and the monthly rent in € per month. 
The levels for naturalness are hardly natural, little natural, partly 
natural, nearly natural, and very natural, which are defined by a 
self-developed graphical scale (see attachment). 
The levels for the walking distance are based on the reported walking 
distance of the respondents in the survey. The levels are -50%, +50%, +100%, 
+200%, and +400% of the actual reported walking distance. The figures are 
presented in absolute values.
The levels for the monthly rent are based on the actual rent reported in the 
survey. The levels are -1%, -0.5%, +0.5%, +1%, +2%, and +5% of the actual 
rent. The figures are presented in absolute values.
Before the choice experiment the respondents were asked about the current 
value of the attributes. This information was used in the choice 
experiment. For example, if a respondent stated the current distance is 
100 meters, the displayed levels in the choice cards are 50m, 150m, 200m, 
300m, 500m. The survey was programmed in a way that the absolute values 
where calculated during survey conduction.

:::


## List the number of alternatives per choice set, the number of choice sets in total and any blocks or randomisation.

*You can use a table here. In cases that the number of alternatives varies, or that you use different split samples for different attributes, elaborate this here.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
There are three alternatives per choice set and 30 choice sets in total. The choice sets are randomly assigned to the respondents, ensuring that each respondent faces ten choice sets.
:::


## How did you code your attributes to generate your design?

*This is specific for your design. Which coding did you use to generate your design. Examples are dummy coding, linear, relative to a status quo, etc.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
In the design, the attributes were coded linearly with the relative values. 
:::



## Did you integrate socio-demographic and other case-specific variables in the design process, and if yes how?


*Case-specific variables are variables that do not vary between alternatives but vary across respondents. These variables could include all variables that you plan to integrate into your utility function, including dummies for split samples. If not applicable, leave blank.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
We need the treatment dummies to test H5. We need the respondent’s city and socio-demographic variables age, gender, income, household size to test H3. These variables were not included in the experimental design.
:::

## Which assumptions on the utility function did you use to generate the design?

*Do you use a utility maximization framework? How do you specify interaction variables? Do you use non-linear specifications of some attributes (e.g. logarithm, quadratic)?*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
We assumed a multinomial logit model, linear and additive in the attributes, with naturalness, walking distance and monthly rent all entering as continuous variables. We assumed respondents choose the alternative giving them the highest utility.
:::

## How did you create your experimental design?

*When you do your design with a specific software (NGENE, `spdesign` in R [@spdesign] etc.), describe all assumptions (utility specification, optimization routine etc.). See for example @scarpa2008design for reporting guidelines of efficient designs.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
The design used was orthogonal. The design included two unlabeled alternatives ("Program 1", "Program 2") and one status quo ("My current situation").
:::

## If an efficient design, which priors did you use, and how did you obtain them?

*State where the priors came from. For example, an assumption about the sign of the parameters, a
pilot, focus groups or expert interviews, or a previous study. If from a pilot, say how
many respondents it had and whether the design was updated afterwards. An efficient
design is only adequate if the priors are approximately right; a design optimised for
the wrong priors can perform worse than an orthogonal one [@walker2018d]. If you are
uncertain, consider a Bayesian efficient design, which integrates over a distribution of
likely parameter values rather than fixed ones [@kessels2006comparison]. See also
@BLIEMER2016. Consider simulations (see next question) to test the designs against different true data generating processes.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
Not applicable. We used an orthogonal design, so no priors entered the design generation. We used the sign expectations from Bronnmann (2023) to check that no choice set contained a dominated alternative.

Bronnmann, Julia, Liebelt, Veronika, Marder, Fabian, Meya, Jasper and Quaas, Martin F., 2023 “The Value of Naturalness of Urban Green Spaces: Evidence From a Discrete Choice Experiment”, Land Economics 
:::

## Did you test the design, e.g., with simulation?

*Monte-Carlo simulations are a good way to test the design for unbiasedness, power and efficiency, and can help you to justify your design choice. In R you can use* `simulateDCE` [@simulateDCE]. *If you did not use simulation, describe how you decided for the design you choose and what other designs you have compared it to.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
The orthogonal design was tested against an efficient and a Bayesian efficient design with priors taken from Bronnmann 2023. We used simulations under different data generating processes. Overall the orthogonal design turned out to be the most robust design, still giving unbiased estimates. The full simulation code is appended to this pre-registration.

Bronnmann, Julia, Liebelt, Veronika, Marder, Fabian, Meya, Jasper and Quaas, Martin F., 2023 “The Value of Naturalness of Urban Green Spaces: Evidence From a Discrete Choice Experiment”, Land Economics
:::

## Do you use an additional split sample approach (between-subject design)?

*Split-sample approaches are frequently used to test methodical research questions or to randomize undesired effects. If you have different versions of your questionnaire that can influence the estimated parameters, explain them and why you used them.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
We apply a split-sample procedure to test the influence of an information treatment. The sample is split into three groups, one uninformed group and two informed groups. The two informed groups differ by how the information is provided. One group is passively provided with information whereas in the other group respondents have to actively decide if they want to be provided with additional information.
In the information treatment, the respondents read an explanatory paragraph of the urban heat island effect accompanied by a graphical illustration. Another paragraph described that the urban heat island effect can be reduced by more naturalness in urban green. Finally, the respondents could voluntarily click to view a 2 minute video on the urban heat island effect. On the next page, the respondents were asked to respond to two self reference questions and two quiz questions. Additionally, we showed some true and false reasons for the heat island effect and asked respondents which of these reasons were true or false.

:::

## Do you randomize the order of choice sets, alternatives and attributes?

*In most cases, it is recommended to randomize the order of choice sets, alternatives and attributes [@mariel2021environmental, pp.40 and 94] to avoid undesired effects (e.g. left right bias). Note down if you do this, or if you do not do this, explain why not.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
We randomise the order of choice sets across respondents. The order of attributes is fixed so that every choice set displays them in the same row order, and the status quo always appears as the third alternative.
:::

## Do you use an opt-out option or a status quo?

*State if you use an opt-out or status quo alternative as an alternative in your choice set. If you do not use any, you can state that you use a forced choice experiment.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
Yes. Each choice set contains the respondent's own status quo alternative alongside the two restructuring programs. We do not use an additional opt-out.
:::

## How do you define the status quo?

*The definition of the status quo is crucial for the interpretation of the results. Note down how it is described to the respondents.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
Respondents first name their most visited urban green space, then report their walking time to it and their current monthly rent, and indicate its naturalness from a set of five graphical illustrations. These answers are piped into the status quo alternative, so each respondent sees their own current situation.
:::

## Are your attributes constant or adapt to the status quo?

*If the status quo is constant for all respondents describe where you got the constant values from. If it varies between respondents, describe how.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
The levels of the naturalness attribute are constant, while the levels for walking distance and monthly rental payment adapt to the status quo.
:::

## Anything else you want to mention regarding experimental design:

*A free text if anything important has not been captured so far.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
No additional remarks.
:::



# Part C: Estimation

Estimation in choice experiments often involves decisions that cannot, and should not, be fixed before seeing the data. This section therefore asks less for binding commitments than for your planned strategy: the models and specifications you intend to explore, the rules you will use to choose among them, and how you will handle deviations if the planned strategy does not work as expected.

## Which software do you use for estimation?

*Name the software and version that you plan to use. If you use different softwares for different purposes or to cross check results, you can describe that here.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
For data preparation we use R. Estimation will be performed using the apollo package in R. Mixed logit models in preference space and willingness to pay space will be cross checked with the Stata functions mixlogit and mixlogitwtp. 
:::


## Which inference criteria do you use?

*Which tests do you apply to test your hypotheses and which significance level do you use to decide on your conclusions. If you do not use formal testing or different testing approaches, describe them.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
We use z-Tests at a 5% level, employing robust standard errors to account for the panel structure in the data. 
:::


## Which discrete choice models do you plan to estimate? If you consider multiple models, specify how you select a model or if a model averaging approach will be used.

*Here, you can list all models that you plan to estimate. Often, the final model choice is an empirical question, and it is totally fine to leave it open which model you will finally use. However, you can still state which models, and which specifications, you estimate and compare to each other. It is also possible to provide a decision tree, containing logical IF-THEN rules.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
We rely on random utility theory and estimate random parameters logit models, conditional logit models, and latent class logit models. We select models based on out-of-sample predictions and measures of fit. If applicable, we use likelihood-ratio tests to compare models.
:::


## Do you estimate in preference space or in willingness to pay space?

*If you derive willingness to pay values, state whether you estimate in preference space or directly in willingness to pay space. The two parameterisations are theoretically equivalent but behave differently in practice: models in preference space can produce poorly behaved, sometimes extreme willingness to pay distributions when the cost coefficient is random, whereas models in willingness to pay space give better behaved welfare estimates but can be harder to converge [@train2005discrete]. If the choice depends on the data, state the criterion you will use to decide.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
We estimate mixed logit models in both preference space and willingness to pay space. We report willingness to pay space as our main specification if the model converges and fit is comparable to the preference space model; otherwise we report preference space and derive willingness to pay from the ratio of coefficients, discussing the resulting distribution.
:::


## Do you control for unobserved and observed heterogeneity, if yes, how (e.g. interactions, membership function in latent class model)?

*Most applications control for unobserved heterogeneity via mixed logit or latent class models and for observed heterogeneity via interaction terms between attributes and alternative-specific constants and case-specific variables such as age or gender. List how you plan to deal with heterogeneity. Guidance on selecting the right model for unobserved heterogeneity can be found in @SAGEBIEL2017. Guidance on choosing distributions in mixed logit specifications can be found in @MARIEL2013*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
We include unobserved preference heterogeneity by estimating a mixed logit model and observed heterogeneity via interaction terms with attributes. For mixed logit models we test different distributions of the random parameters. For latent class logit models, we determine the optimal class sizes based on parameter plausibility and BIC. For testing interaction terms, we use likelihood-ratio tests. 
:::


## Do you estimate separate models for different groups?

*To compare different groups, one can either use interaction terms or estimate separate models for each group. Elaborate if you want to estimate separate models and how you want to compare estimates between models.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
We estimate one model for each of the 14 cities where we are conducting the choice experiment and one model for all respondents. We also estimate separate models for the different treatments.
:::

## Do you derive any welfare measures and how?

*Welfare measures can be compensated or equivalent measures, willingness to pay, willingness to accept or others. Explain which ones you want to use and how you calculate them.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
We derive marginal willingness to pay for naturalness and walking distance as the ratio of the attribute coefficient to the rent coefficient. In willingness to pay space we estimate these ratios directly. For preference space models, we report standard errors and confidence intervals from the delta method.
:::


## If methodical research question, describe in detail how you test your methodical hypotheses.

*There are different approaches to approach methodical research questions. Often, researchers use split samples and then compare results between them using separate models or interaction terms. Explain how you approach your methodical research question and how you plan to test it.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
We want to compare the effects of the different information treatments. To do so, we estimate separate models and compare coefficients with Poe and Z-tests. Further we estimate a pooled model with treatment dummy interaction terms.
:::


## Describe any additional exploratory analysis you have planned to conduct.

*Sometimes, you have already some other ideas on what to do with the data but are not specific about it. Here, you can elaborate on this.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
The survey included a block on nature relatedness with 6 items. We want to include a nature relatedness index as interaction terms in a mixed logit model and also model nature relatedness and choices simultaneously with hybrid choice models.
:::


## Anything else you want to mention regarding estimation:

*A free text if anything important has not been captured so far.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
No additional remarks.
:::


# Part D: Validity

## Do you use any measures to enhance validity and reduce hypothetical bias?

*The stated preferences literature suffers from validity issues and hypothetical bias and other biases. Several measures have been developed to counteract these biases. Explain in detail which ones you use and if not, why not. See @johnston2017contemporary for best practices.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
We include questions on consequentiality perceptions after the choice experiment, employ cheap talk scripts, and conduct ex-ante and ex-post validations of respondent understanding.
:::


## Which follow up questions do you use?

*To ex-post assess the validity of your results, you can use follow up questions, e.g. on consequentiality, comprehension and credibility, how the respondent made their choices, which attributes were perceived etc.*

::: {.content-visible when-profile="answers"}
We included questions on perceived consequentiality.
:::
